lesson.title: Talent or Training? Dweck's Contested Theory of Mindset
lesson.summary: Carol Dweck's fixed and growth mindsets describe beliefs about whether ability is a fixed trait or something that can be developed, an influential idea in education that later research has shown to have real but more modest effects than originally popularized.
lesson.body:
A fixed mindset is the belief that qualities like intelligence and talent are fixed traits, you either have them or you don't. A growth mindset is the belief that those same qualities can be developed over time through effort, good strategies, and learning from mistakes. Carol Dweck's research popularized this distinction and connected it to real differences in how people respond to challenge and failure.

This isn't the same thing as intelligence itself; the g factor you covered earlier describes how ability actually differs and correlates across tasks. Mindset is a belief about ability, not a measure of it, and it interacts closely with self-efficacy: what you believe is possible to become capable at shapes how much effort and persistence you're willing to invest, which in turn shapes your actual belief in your ability to succeed at a given attempt.

In some of the best-known studies, Dweck and colleagues found that children praised for their intelligence after succeeding at a task, being told something like 'you're so smart,' later tended to avoid harder challenges, showed less persistence after failure, and were more likely to interpret a poor performance as proof that they simply weren't smart. Children praised instead for their effort or strategy tended to seek out harder challenges and stay more persistent after setbacks, treating a poor performance as information about what to try differently rather than as a verdict on their ability. This gave rise to the popular classroom advice to praise effort and process rather than fixed traits.

It's important to be honest about where this research stands today. Growth mindset became hugely influential in education, but larger and more recent studies have complicated the original picture. Large-scale replications and meta-analyses have generally found real but fairly modest effects of mindset on academic achievement on average, with the strongest and most reliable benefits often concentrated among students who are academically at-risk or who face structural disadvantages, rather than a large effect across all students. Some individual findings from the early wave of mindset research have also proven hard to replicate at the original effect sizes. None of this means the core idea is wrong; the general finding that believing effort can improve ability tends to support more persistence than believing ability is fixed still holds up reasonably well, but growth mindset should be treated as an influential and partly supported theory still under active scientific debate, not as a settled, guaranteed fix for underachievement.
